transfer_rules.rule_summary: The UK abolished exchange controls in 1979, so you do not need government approval to move money into or out of the UK. Normal bank checks and the cash declaration rule still apply.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Exchange control was introduced into the United Kingdom shortly before the outbreak of the 1939-45 war and was abolished on 24 October 1979.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Declare cash of £10,000 or more at the border
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If you carry £10,000 or more in cash (or the equivalent) into or out of Great Britain from a country outside the UK, you must declare it to UK customs. Groups travelling together must declare if their combined total reaches £10,000.
documents_required: Cash declaration made online or by phone (earliest 72 hours before travel), or in person to Border Force via the red channel / 'goods to declare' on arrival
transfer_rules.restrictions: Cash includes notes and coins, bearer bonds, travellers' cheques and signed cheques not made out to a named person or organisation. If you fail to declare, all the cash you are carrying can be seized, and you may have to pay a penalty of up to £5,000 to get it back.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Northern Ireland uses a €10,000 threshold for cash moving between Northern Ireland and non-EU countries and for cash arriving from Great Britain; for Northern Ireland movements, money orders, gold coins or bullion and prepaid cards also count as cash. No declaration is needed for cash going from Northern Ireland to Great Britain.
transfer_rules.regulator: HM Revenue & Customs and Border Force (Home Office)
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: You must declare cash of £10,000 or more to UK customs

transfer_rules.rule_name: Cash of any amount can be seized on suspicion of crime
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Even below £10,000, customs can seize cash if they have reasonable grounds to suspect a crime. They can hold it for 48 hours, after which they need a court order to keep it.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Cash can be held for 48 hours; longer detention requires a court order. Appeals against a penalty must be made within 30 days of the penalty notice.
transfer_rules.regulator: HM Revenue & Customs and Border Force (Home Office)
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Any cash can be seized if customs authorities have reasonable grounds to suspect a crime.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Avoid bringing large amounts of cash; check home-country limits
transfer_rules.rule_summary: UKCISA strongly advises international students not to bring large amounts of cash and to use a debit or credit card instead. You should also check whether your home country restricts how much cash you can take out.
transfer_rules.regulator: UK Council for International Student Affairs (UKCISA) - advisory body
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: whether the country where you live has any restrictions on cash that may be taken out of the country.

transfer_rules.rule_name: Pay tuition fees by bank transfer, arranged with your university
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Rather than carrying cash for fees, contact your university before you leave home and ask whether you can pay your fees in advance by bank transfer. If that is not possible, ask the university about other payment methods.
transfer_rules.regulator: UK Council for International Student Affairs (UKCISA) - advisory body
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: contact your institution before you leave home and ask if you can pay your fees in advance, by bank transfer.

transfer_rules.nationality_condition: Not required upfront for British National (Overseas) applicants and nationals of listed countries (e.g. Australia, Canada, Japan, USA), though UKVI may still request evidence
transfer_rules.residency_condition: Not required if you have lived in the UK with a visa for at least 12 months before applying
transfer_rules.visa_condition: Student visa applicants studying in London
transfer_rules.rule_name: Student visa living-cost funds (London): £1,529 per month
transfer_rules.rule_summary: To get a Student visa for a course in London you must show £1,529 per month for living costs (for up to 9 months), on top of your first-year course fees shown on your CAS.
documents_required: Bank or building society statements, passbook, certificate of deposit or bank letter
Evidence of course fees for 1 academic year (amount shown on the CAS)
If using a parent's money: a letter from the parent confirming you may use it
transfer_rules.restrictions: Amount is per month for up to 9 months. Extra funds are required for each dependant (£845 per month in London). Overdrafts, cryptocurrency, stocks and shares, pensions and unregulated accounts cannot be used.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Student union sabbatical officers and applicants who have lived in the UK with a visa for at least 12 months are exempt. Some nationalities need not provide evidence upfront unless asked.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: £1,529 per month (for up to 9 months) for courses in London

transfer_rules.nationality_condition: Not required upfront for British National (Overseas) applicants and nationals of listed countries (e.g. Australia, Canada, Japan, USA), though UKVI may still request evidence
transfer_rules.residency_condition: Not required if you have lived in the UK with a visa for at least 12 months before applying
transfer_rules.visa_condition: Student visa applicants studying outside London
transfer_rules.rule_name: Student visa living-cost funds (outside London): £1,171 per month
transfer_rules.rule_summary: To get a Student visa for a course outside London you must show £1,171 per month for living costs (for up to 9 months), on top of your first-year course fees shown on your CAS.
documents_required: Bank or building society statements, passbook, certificate of deposit or bank letter
Evidence of course fees for 1 academic year (amount shown on the CAS)
If using a parent's money: a letter from the parent confirming you may use it
transfer_rules.restrictions: Amount is per month for up to 9 months. Extra funds are required for each dependant (£680 per month outside London). Overdrafts, cryptocurrency, stocks and shares, pensions and unregulated accounts cannot be used.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Student union sabbatical officers and applicants who have lived in the UK with a visa for at least 12 months are exempt. Some nationalities need not provide evidence upfront unless asked.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: £1,171 per month (for up to 9 months) for courses outside London

transfer_rules.visa_condition: Student visa applicants who must show funds
transfer_rules.rule_name: 28-day rule for visa proof of funds
transfer_rules.rule_summary: The required money must sit in the account for at least 28 days in a row, and the end of that 28-day period must be within 31 days of the date you apply for your visa. If the balance dips below the required amount on any day, the evidence will not meet the rule.
documents_required: Statements or bank letter covering 28 consecutive days, with the closing balance date no more than 31 days before the application
transfer_rules.restrictions: The account must give immediate access to the money; a parent's or partner's account must be one they control.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Same exemptions as the maintenance requirement (12 months' UK residence on a visa, sabbatical officers, listed nationalities unless asked).
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: You must have this money for at least 28 days in a row. The end date of the 28-day period must be within 31 days of the date you apply for your visa.

transfer_rules.visa_condition: Student visa applicants who must show funds
transfer_rules.rule_name: Funds in foreign currency converted at OANDA spot rate
transfer_rules.rule_summary: You can show visa funds held in a foreign currency. UKVI converts them to pounds using the OANDA spot rate on the date you apply, so keep a buffer in case the exchange rate moves against you.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: If the money is in a foreign currency, we will convert it to British pounds using the spot exchange rate on OANDA for the date of the application.

transfer_rules.visa_condition: Applicants who need immigration permission must hold it; overstayers cannot open a current account
transfer_rules.rule_name: Banks must check identity and immigration status
transfer_rules.rule_summary: UK banks must see proof of identity and run an immigration status check on everyone who applies for a current account. Someone without the immigration permission they need (an overstayer) cannot open one.
documents_required: Proof of immigration status, e.g. eVisa share code (BRPs have been replaced by eVisas)
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Banks and building societies must make a status check on all new applicants for a current account.

transfer_rules.rule_summary: When you pay a UK account, your bank checks the name you typed against the account. You will see a match, a close match (with the real name shown), no match, or 'unable to check'; on no match, contact the person or organisation before paying.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Covers domestic UK payments only; it does not check international payments.
transfer_rules.exceptions: If the receiving organisation does not offer CoP, you get an 'unable to be checked' result.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Confirmation of Payee (CoP) is an account name-checking service designed to help reduce misdirected payments

transfer_rules.rule_name: Reimbursement if tricked into a UK bank transfer (APP fraud)
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If a fraudster tricks you into sending money by UK bank transfer (Faster Payments or CHAPS) on or after 7 October 2024, your bank must generally reimburse you up to £85,000. Report it as soon as possible and within 13 months.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Applies to UK bank transfers via Faster Payments or CHAPS; card, cash and cheque payments have separate protections. Firms may apply an excess of up to £100 (not to vulnerable consumers). Claims must be made within 13 months of the payment.
transfer_rules.exceptions: International transfers are outside the stated scope (UK bank transfers only). Losses above £85,000 can be taken to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: These measures apply to UK bank transfers.

transfer_rules.rule_name: When a bank can refuse a payment
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Your bank can only refuse a payment if you lack funds, it breaks the account terms, or it would be against the law, and it must generally tell you as soon as possible and, where it can, why.
transfer_rules.restrictions: The bank may charge a fee if a refusal is reasonably justified.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: Your bank can only refuse to make a payment if:

transfer_rules.rule_name: Never let others move money through your account (money mules)
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If you let someone pay money into your account and pass it on, you become a 'money mule' and are taking part in money laundering, which is a crime. The FCA warns this could carry a prison sentence of up to 14 years.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Do not let anyone you don't know deposit money into your account or ask you to transfer it on.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: As a money mule you are involved in money laundering, which is a criminal offence.

transfer_rules.rule_summary: UK banks are subject to anti-money-laundering rules and may ask questions about large or unusual payments. A consumer-facing official statement of when and what they ask could not be confirmed.

account_opening.summary: Any UK bank must see proof of identity and run an immigration status check before opening a current account, so an international student needs a passport and proof of immigration permission (now an eVisa, shared via a share code). Most banks also ask for proof of address, and many accept a university bank letter for it. Several major banks only offer their standard student account to people who have lived in the UK for 3 years or more. International students are pointed to dedicated international student accounts (HSBC, Lloyds, Santander) or to basic or standard accounts instead.
typical_documents: eVisa share code or other proof of immigration status (BRPs have been replaced by eVisas)
Proof of UK address, e.g. university banking letter, utility bill or bank statement dated within the last 3 months
Letter from your university confirming your student status and course (letter of introduction / bank letter)
Proof of acceptance onto a qualifying course (e.g. HSBC International Student Bank Account)
Selfie or short video for identity checks when applying through an app (NatWest, Barclays)
eligibility_factors: Valid immigration permission: banks must not open a current account for an overstayer
UK residence: Lloyds, Santander and NatWest require you to live in the UK; NatWest says non-residents cannot open an account
Length of UK residence: Barclays and NatWest student accounts require at least 3 years' UK residence, which rules out most international students
Minimum age: usually 18 (NatWest student account 17+; Santander international student page says 16+)
Enrolment on a qualifying full-time course at a UK university or college
Credit check consent for some accounts (e.g. Barclays Student Additions)
Basic bank accounts usually have no fees and no overdraft and may suit people refused a standard account

documents: Proof of address, e.g. bill or bank statement dated within the last 3 months
Proof of acceptance onto a qualifying course at a UK university or college
banks.credit_card_available: HSBC Student Credit Card (up to £250) requires being over 18, a UK resident, and holding an HSBC Student Bank Account. HSBC says getting a credit card as an international student 'can be hard'. The International Student Bank Account itself has no credit, overdraft or cheque book.
banks.evidence_quote: Our current account for international students.
banks.notes: HSBC's international page says you can open an HSBC Bank Account whether you're new to the UK or 'haven't arrived just yet', and lets you 'send and receive money to over 150 destinations outside the UK'. Gives access to customer-only products such as the Global Money Account. The dedicated product page (hsbc.co.uk/current-accounts/products/international-student/) could not be fetched, so visa and residence requirements are unconfirmed.

banks.account_type: Student Additions account (UK-resident students); international students directed to the standard Barclays Bank Account
documents: Short video of yourself for ID checks
Course details and UCAS status code
Postgraduates: letter from your university confirming course details (in branch)
banks.monthly_fee: No charge to open or use the student account
banks.evidence_quote: you can't apply to a student account if you haven't been a UK resident for 3+ years
banks.notes: Student Additions requires at least 3 years' UK residence and full-time study; interest-free arranged overdraft up to £500 in the first term, £1,000 in year 1 and £1,500 from year 2 (UK students). The student page says international students can apply for a standard Barclays account in the app, but the Barclays Bank Account and Basic Account pages list 'Are 18 or older and not in full-time education' and require a UK mobile number and home address. That conflict needs checking with Barclays.

documents: Proof of identity if not an existing Lloyds customer
banks.evidence_quote: Yes, you can transfer money from an international bank account.
banks.notes: Requirements include being 18 or over and living in the UK. For an incoming international transfer you usually need the account holder's name, IBAN or account number and SWIFT/BIC. Lloyds' New to UK page says a non-UK passport is accepted 'mobile banking app only' and that international addresses are accepted. Overdraft and visa requirements are not stated.

Proof of address, e.g. utility bill, bank statement, UCAS letter, Student Finance letter or university letter

bureaus: Crediva (listed by MoneyHelper as a fourth agency)
what_contributes: Credit accounts and payment history, including missed or late payments and defaults
Current account data shared by major UK lenders
Service and utility accounts (monthly energy/water contracts, not prepayment meters)
Public records such as County Court Judgments
Hard searches made when you apply for credit
Linked people such as joint borrowers, and previous addresses
Rent payments, if added through a third-party service
why_it_matters: Banks and lenders use your report to decide whether to lend to you or open an account
Mobile providers may check your report before offering a contract (not for pay-as-you-go)
Gas and electricity suppliers may check it before offering contracts
Landlords can check your report, though they usually see only public record information
Credit reference data is used to verify identity, age and residency and to detect fraud
A good history makes credit easier and cheaper to get
responsible_behaviours: Register on the electoral roll if you are eligible (UK, Irish, qualifying Commonwealth citizens with leave to enter or remain, and some EU citizens)
Open and run a UK current account well, routing bills through it
Put household bills in your name and pay by direct debit on time
Use a monthly mobile contract in your name rather than pay-as-you-go
If you use a credit or credit builder card, pay the full balance on time each month and keep usage to about 25% of your limit
Space out credit applications by several months
Check your credit report regularly for errors or identity theft; you can request it free from any agency
risks: Missed or late payments and defaults stay on your report for up to six years
Many hard searches in a short time can make lenders see you as higher risk
Applying for credit you are not eligible for, and repeated rejections, can harm your score
Credit builder cards often have low limits and high interest if not paid in full
Moving house often can lower your score
Debts owed abroad can still follow you even though the credit history does not
credit_system.foreigner_notes: Overseas credit history does not transfer to the UK, so newcomers start with no file ('credit invisible') or a thin one and must build a UK history from scratch. Building enough history can take up to six months after opening accounts. Many international students cannot join the electoral register: it is open to UK, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens with leave to remain, plus some EU citizens, so other nationals should rely on a UK bank account, monthly bills and contracts in their own name. HSBC says getting a credit card as an international student 'can be hard', and its Student Credit Card requires UK residency.
